#### What we are learning today

Last time we learned that NFAs and DFAs are equivalent.  Today we will
learn that any language that can be represented by a regular expression
can also be recognized by an NFA.

$$
\Large
\begin{array}{ccc}
\mathrm{DFA} & \stackrel{4/17}{\longleftrightarrow} & \mathrm{NFA} \\
& \nearrow & \\
\mathrm{regular} &&\\
\mathrm{expression}  &&
\end{array}
$$


Eventually, we want to add regular grammars to our picture, and add some more arrows.

$$
\Large
\begin{array}{ccc}
\mathrm{DFA} & \stackrel{4/17}\longleftrightarrow & \mathrm{NFA} \\
& \nearrow & \\
\mathrm{regular}& & \mathrm{regular} \\
\mathrm{expression}& & \mathrm{grammar} 
\end{array}
$$

We will see that all of these are equivalent.  The languages recognized/generated/expressed
by DFAs/NFAs/regular grammars/regular expressions are called **regular langauges**.

<div class = "foldable" label = "Exercise 3.6.21">
Last time we created an equivalent DFA by drawing its graph.
This time, I'll demonstrate another way to keep track of the work involved
using a transition table rather than a graph. I'll try to remember to
record this so those of you not in class (or wanting to rewatch it) 
can view it in Teams.

To create a transition table for a DFA, we need to show for each combination
of a state and an input symbol which state we transition to.  (Since it is
a DFA, there will be just one state. But the states of the DFA are 
subsets of states from the NFA.  I'll show the table here using two 
different notations, one that makes the sets explicit and one that
is a little terser.)


The transition tables are here for reference, but you should watch the video
to see how these are created step-by-step.

<div class = "foldable" label = "transition table">

\def\set#1{\{#1\}}

Explicit sets version:

  state            |      0      |       1     
:----------------: | :---------: | :----------:
$\set{A}$ (start)  | $\set{A, C}$  | $\set{B}$
$\set{A, C}$       | $\set{A, C}$  | $\set{B, D}$
$\set{B}$          | $\set{A, C}$  | $\set{C}$
$\set{B,D}$        | $\set{B, D}$  | $\set{A,C}$
$\set{C}$          | $\set{C}$     | $\set{D}$
$\set{D}$          | $\set{D}$     | $\set{A}$

Terser version:

  state            |      0      |       1     
:----------------: | :---------: | :----------:
$A$ (start)        | $AC$        | $B$
$AC$               | $AC$        | $BD$
$B$                | $AC$        | $C$
$BD$               | $BD$       | $AC$
$C$                | $C$         | $D$
$D$                | $D$         | $A$

Once we get to this point, it is easy to draw the graph if we like.  We know the
6 states that are required, and we can use the chart to decide where the arrows
go. (Note: the transition table is a complete description of the DFA, so
the graph is not necessary -- unless asked for.)
</div>
</div>

<div class = "foldable" label = "Exercise 4.3.5">
See pages 881-882 in the text for an explanation and illustration.
Make sure you understand the big idea for each one, then see if there are any
smaller details that are important to remember.

Big idea:

* $AB$: Hook up the machine one after the other, and provide a way to get from the
first to the second whenever you could have gone to an accepting state in the first machine.

One note: Below the illustration for $AB$ it says
"Transition from $s_B$ in $M_B$ produces a transition from $s_{AB} = s_A$."
This transition should only be added **if the start state for $M_A$ is an accepting state.**
In that case, we need to be able to recognize $\lambda w = w$ for any $w \in B = L(M_B)$.
But if the start state for $M_A$ is not accepting, then $\lambda \not\in A$, and we do 
not want to recognize these strings (unless they can be split some other way into a 
first part from $A$ and a second part from $B$>)
</div>

<div class = "foldable" label = "Exercise 4.3.6">
See pages 881-882 in the text for an explanation and illustration.
Make sure you understand the big idea for each one, then see if there are any
smaller details that are important to remember.

Big idea:

* $A \union B$: Hook up the machines "in parallel" and make a first decision about which machine
to use.

</div>

<div class = "foldable" label = "Exercise 4.3.7">
See pages 881-882 in the text for an explanation and illustration.
Make sure you understand the big idea for each one, then see if there are any
smaller details that are important to remember.

Big idea:

* $A^*$: Provide a way to "start over" any time you reach an accepting state.
</div>
